verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 76 (Gita Press/Poddar, Haritoshini and Thakur all number it 76); the quoted lines are stanza 3 of a 4-stanza pada that opens 'राम को गुलाम, नाम रामबोला राख्यो राम'.
attribution_note: Tulsidas speaking of himself to Ram (and, in stanza 4, to the people who call him low). Listener 'Ram' is fine.
translation_note: First half is right. The last clause 'बोलि सेबक-सुखद, सदा बिरद बहत हौं' is read by both Poddar and Viyogi Hari with Tulsidas as subject: since that day he has always worn the Lord's badge/insignia (the Vaishnava marks: kanthi, tilak, the name) that gladdens devotees. Our version makes Ram the one who 'carries that name'. Suggest: 'He spoke to me, and ever since I have worn the badge of the one who gladdens his servants.' Also 'मींजो गुरु पीठ': both commentators take 'guru' as Ram himself as the supreme teacher, so 'Like a teacher' is acceptable but 'my teacher, Ram, patted my back' is closer.
context: Pada 76 is one of Tulsidas's autobiographical petitions: he calls himself Ram's slave, named Rambola, who gets food and clothing for saying the name now and then. He recalls being bound by his own deeds and pride, crying out, and being freed; then the moment of acceptance (our lines). The pada ends with him shrugging off people who call him low: he wants no marriage alliance or caste standing, and lives content trusting Ram's love.

key_terms.sense: servant, bondsman; Viyogi Hari insists elsewhere it means servant, not disciple
I have no one of my own anywhere: the orphan's plea
the guru (Ram as teacher) stroked/patted my back, i.e. reassured and steadied me
took me by the arm: the gesture of accepting someone as one's own
I bear the badge/insignia, i.e. wear the devotee's marks as one now belonging to Ram

core_teaching: Belonging is given, not earned: a person with no one says plainly 'I want to be yours, I have no one', and is taken by the arm and owned. Once owned, other people's verdicts (low, outcaste) stop mattering.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads the whole pada as Tulsi's story: bound by karma and pride, he cried out; Ram, seeing him burn, freed him; asked who he was, he begged to be his servant.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls the pada Tulsi's own 'Ram-story'; notes he treats Ram and guru as one, citing Kabir on the guru.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the scene as the guru touching and caressing his back, taking his arms and making him his own, after Tulsi says he has no one and clings to the feet.

practical_reading: For someone who feels without family or standing, the pada models saying the need out loud ('I have no one') and letting oneself be claimed; a teacher's hand on the back is the picture of being steadied, not judged.
misreadings: Not a claim that Tulsidas's social rejection was deserved or that caste does not hurt; he refuses to let it define him.
Not a story of earning acceptance through practice: he is taken in at the moment he asks.
cautions: Autobiographical details (orphanhood, being called low) may surface a reader's own family rejection.
The full pada dismisses marriage and caste ties; avoid presenting that as advice for a reader's relationships.
speaks_to: feeling you have no one anywhere
being newly accepted somewhere after a long time alone
people looking down on you for your background
needing a mentor's reassurance
not_for: someone grieving a specific person, where 'I have no one' could deepen isolation without the turn
readers in conflict over marriage or family duties (the full pada brushes those aside)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 78, final couplet (stanza 6) of the pada that opens 'दीन को दयालु दानि दूसरो न कोऊ' (Haritoshini 78; Thakur 78). The Gita Press 2001 scan's OCR for this pada could not be located.
translation_note: Accurate. 'निवाज' is to favour/enrich (Viyogi Hari: make the poor fulfilled), so 'lifts up' is fine. 'बारक' = just once.
context: The pada argues that Ram is the only giver worth asking: everyone else Tulsi tells his poverty to turns out to be poor too; gods, men and sages are masters only until Ram turns his eyes away. Ram has made stones, beasts, trees and birds his own and turned paupers into kings. The ending (our lines) narrows to one request: say once that Tulsidas is yours.

key_terms.sense: one who favours and raises the poor
I am your poor one: claims a relationship, not just need
'Tulsidas is mine': the word of ownership he wants to hear

core_teaching: The deepest request is not for things but to be claimed: one word from the beloved, 'you are mine', outweighs every gift.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains: whoever I tell my need to proves needy himself; one who begs from Ram never begs again. Ending: you raise the poor and I am your poor servant, so say just once 'Tulsidas is mine'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as a plea to the compassionate one to say just once that Tulsidasa is his, after listing the stone, tree, bird and beast he made his own.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to name a need under many needs: to be acknowledged as belonging to someone. It invites a reader to say what they actually want to hear.
misreadings: Not a statement that poverty is a virtue or should be accepted passively.
cautions: A reader who longs to hear 'you are mine' from a parent or partner who will not say it may feel the ache sharply; keep the reading pointed toward being held by the divine, not toward forcing a person.
speaks_to: wanting to be acknowledged, not just helped
feeling poor or small next to others
longing for belonging
not_for: someone in a coercive relationship who is told to wait for a word of ownership
research_note: Gita Press 2001 OCR text for pada 78 could not be located (only two sources used).

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 79, complete (4 stanzas) - same number and text in Gita Press/Poddar, Haritoshini and Thakur.
translation_note: Faithful. 'चेरो' = servant/slave (Viyogi Hari explicitly rejects reading it as 'disciple'). 'ब्रह्म तू, हौं जीव' is rendered 'you are the infinite, I a small life' - acceptable; commentators keep it as Brahman/jiva.
context: A short, complete pada built from paired opposites: kind one and needy one, giver and beggar, sin-remover and famous sinner, Brahman and jiva, master and servant. It ends by leaving the choice of relationship to Ram, asking only that Tulsi find shelter at his feet by any route.

key_terms.sense: the needy one and the compassionate one: each half of a pair needs the other
you are Brahman, I am the individual soul

core_teaching: Every lack in the devotee matches a quality in God, so weakness becomes a reason for closeness rather than distance; the form of the relationship matters less than reaching shelter.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes the pairs one by one: you are the giver and I the beggar, the protector of orphans and none is more orphaned than I; you are mother, father, guru, friend and benefactor.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds a note that 'chero' means servant or slave, correcting Rameshwar Bhatt's gloss 'disciple'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the list as Brahman and bound soul, master and slave, and 'father, mother, teacher, friend' as benefactor in every way; take whichever bond you fancy.

practical_reading: Used to show that one can come to God through whatever relationship feels natural - child, friend, servant - and that admitting one's poverty is itself the opening.
misreadings: Not self-hatred: 'famous sinner' is a devotional convention that sets up the matching quality in Ram.
Not a fixed hierarchy that the reader must adopt; the pada explicitly leaves the choice of bond open.
cautions: The 'father and mother' line may sting for someone estranged from or recently bereaved of a parent; it can also comfort. Handle gently.
speaks_to: feeling you bring nothing but need
wanting a relationship with God but unsure what form
feeling alone with no protector
not_for: someone working to stop harsh self-talk, if the 'sinner' pairs are read literally

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 101, first line(s) of a 3-stanza pada (Gita Press/Poddar 101, Haritoshini 101, Thakur 101).
translation_note: Accurate for the refrain and first line.
context: The pada asks where else Tulsi could go: which other deity has made a point of seeking out the lowest to save them, and has freed a bird (Jatayu), beasts, a hunter (Valmiki), a stone (Ahalya), trees (the Yamalarjuna) and a foreigner? Gods, demons, sages, nagas and humans are themselves held by maya, so why hand oneself over to them?

key_terms.sense: to whom the very lowly are especially dear
picking them out one by one, for the sake of his own pledge

core_teaching: Refuge is sought where there is a record of saving the fallen; the devotee turns to Ram because Ram, unlike the bound beings around, is free to free others.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks who else bears the name 'purifier of the fallen' and loves the lowly; lists the bird, beasts, hunter Valmiki, stone Ahalya, trees and Yavana as those saved.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; glosses 'barai' as picking out one by one. Cites Gita 18.61 (the Lord turning all beings on the machine of maya) and the Manas line that Ram makes all dance like puppets, to explain why others cannot save.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: where should I go save your feet, who else is the fallen ones' redeemer and insists on saving sinner after sinner for his name's sake.

practical_reading: Teachers use the opening line as a song of exclusive trust: when other supports have failed, go back to the one whose nature is to lift the fallen.
misreadings: Not a polemic for a reader to look down on other faiths or deities; it is Tulsi's personal reason for his one refuge.
cautions: The full pada calls other gods 'poor things' under maya; avoid quoting that part in an interfaith or mixed-family context.
speaks_to: feeling you have nowhere else to go
feeling too fallen to be loved
wanting to return after drifting
not_for: readers from other traditions if the comparative stanza is used

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 102, stanzas 1 and 5 (of 5) - same in Gita Press/Poddar and Haritoshini.
translation_note: Accurate for the two quoted lines. Note the omitted middle (fish-and-hook image) carries the request the setting mentions ('asks for one more thing').
context: Tulsi thanks Hari for the human body, the home of every spiritual practice, and says he cannot recount even one favour with a million mouths, yet he asks for more. His mind is a fish that never leaves the water of sense pleasures, so he keeps suffering birth after birth; he asks Ram to make grace the line, the goad-mark on his foot the hook and supreme love the bait, and pull the fish out. Many remedies and gods exist, but only the one who tied the rope of delusion can untie it.

key_terms.sense: the human body as the home/base of all spiritual practice
hard to obtain even for the gods
the mind as a fish that cannot leave the water of sense objects
the one who bound it is the one who unbinds

core_teaching: Human life is a rare gift for practice, but a mind hooked on pleasures cannot free itself by effort alone; release comes from the same higher power that holds the soul in the world.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the fish image: make your grace the string, the ankusha mark on your foot the hook, supreme love the soft bait, and pierce and draw out my mind-fish; it is play for you.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls the pada doctrinal and its image unmatched; reads the last line as: the Lord of maya who tied the soul with ignorance and sent it into the world will himself release it.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the close as there being many Vedic remedies and gods, but the noose of delusion can be loosed only by the one who tied it.

practical_reading: Gratitude and asking can sit together: be thankful for a human life, then admit honestly what you cannot fix yourself (a compulsion, a craving) and ask for help.
misreadings: Not a claim that God caused a person's specific suffering or addiction to punish them.
Not permission to stop effort; the rest of the Vinaya Patrika asks for both effort and grace.
cautions: 'The one who tied this knot' can be heard by someone in pain as 'God did this to you'; frame it as the power that holds us also frees us.
Rebirth language ('born in many wombs') in the full pada.
speaks_to: being stuck in a habit or craving you cannot break
feeling grateful for life yet still restless
having tried many remedies
not_for: someone in acute addiction crisis needing practical help, if used instead of it
someone angry at God over a loss (the 'binder' line may inflame)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 103, stanzas 1 and 3 (of 4) - same in Gita Press/Poddar, Haritoshini and Thakur.
translation_note: Accurate. 'जीव-जड़ताई' is glossed by Poddar as the foolishness of relying on other means, gods or deeds, and by Viyogi Hari as the soul's ignorance; 'dullness of this soul' is fine. The omitted stanza 2 (asking for no liberation, wealth or powers, only motiveless love) is the heart of the 'steady love' setting.
context: A complete short prayer. Tulsi asks Ram to remove every other hope and reliance; he wants no good afterlife, clever mind, wealth, powers or fame, only love for Ram's feet that grows daily and asks nothing. Wherever his crooked deeds drag him, birth after birth, let Ram's care not lapse for a moment, as the tortoise never forgets her eggs. Finally he asks that all the love and ties of this body be gathered into one place, in Ram.

key_terms.sense: hope, trust and reliance (placed in anything other than Ram)
love without a motive; Viyogi Hari: love for a return is shopkeeping, not love
crooked karma dragging one by force
like the tortoise with her eggs: care at a distance, by attention alone

core_teaching: Ask not for outcomes but for undivided, motiveless love, and for God's attention to stay with you even where your own mistakes take you.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads the first line as asking Ram to remove the folly of trusting other means, gods or actions; Tulsi wants no good destiny, wealth or powers, only ever-growing pure love.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that love with a motive is trade, not love.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea that wherever his evil karmas dispose him he may not lose the Lord's love, as the mother-turtle never leaves her eggs.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to shift prayer from 'fix my circumstances' to 'stay with me in them'; even when habits pull you somewhere you regret, ask not to be left alone there.
misreadings: Not fatalism about karma: the point is being accompanied, not that effort is useless.
'Take away every other hope' is not advice to cut off human relationships; stanza 4 asks that those loves be gathered into the divine, not destroyed.
cautions: Mentions being dragged through many births by bad karma; may feel heavy to someone already blaming themselves.
speaks_to: fear that your own mistakes will take you somewhere you can't come back from
wanting love that isn't transactional
asking to be watched over from a distance
not_for: someone who needs concrete help and hears 'drop all other reliance' as 'don't seek help'

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 105, refrain and first line (of 3 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 105, Haritoshini 105, Thakur 105.
translation_note: Accurate. 'नसानी' = has been spoiled/wasted; 'डसैहौं' = I will spread (bedding); both commentators read the bed as maya's snare.
context: Tulsi's vow of a fresh start. By Ram's grace the night of worldly life has passed, and having woken he will not lay out the bed again. He has found the name as a wish-fulfilling gem and will not let it drop from the hand of his heart; he will test the gold of his mind on the dark touchstone of Ram's form; the senses mocked him while he was their slave, but now, his own master, he will not be laughed at; he will set his mind like a bee on Ram's lotus feet.

key_terms.sense: till now it was ruined; from now I won't let it be
I won't spread the bed again, i.e. won't fall back into the sleep of illusion
touchstone, the dark stone gold is tested on; Ram's dark form as the test of the mind

core_teaching: Waking up is a gift of grace, but staying awake is a resolve: don't relitigate the wasted years, just refuse to lie back down.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: my life so far was wasted, but no more; Ram's grace ended the night of worldly maya, and awake I will not spread maya's bedding again.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads the first line as 'what I did so far is spoiled, from now I'll take care'; equates it with the proverb 'forget what has passed, look after what lies ahead'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: I have wasted my time long enough, now no more; the night of existence has passed by Rama's grace and, awake, I'll make my bed no more.

practical_reading: Used for fresh starts: name the lost time honestly, credit the waking to grace rather than willpower, and make one concrete resolve not to slide back.
misreadings: Not self-condemnation over the past; the commentators read it as 'let bygones go and look ahead'.
Not a promise that relapse can't happen; it is a vow, not a guarantee.
cautions: 'Till now it has been wasted' could sting for someone ashamed of years lost to illness or addiction; stress the second half.
speaks_to: regret over lost years
a turning point or new start
waking up from a habit or a numb period
not_for: someone in depression for whom 'just wake up and resolve' may feel like blame

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 125 (a 9-line chaupai-style pada); our text quotes lines 2, 8 and 9 - Gita Press/Poddar 125, Haritoshini 125, Thakur 125.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Tulsi complains to Ram, the steady benefactor: his heart is Ram's house, but thieves have moved in - ignorance, delusion, greed, ego, intoxication/pride, anger and lust, 'the enemy of understanding'. They bully him, ignore his pleas, trample him as an orphan; he is one and they are many, no one hears him, and running away won't help. So he tells Ram: it is your house they are looting; my only worry is your bad name.

key_terms.sense: the heart is the Lord's own dwelling
thieves: the seven inner enemies listed in the pada
Mara (Kama, desire), the enemy of understanding (Viyogi Hari's reading)

core_teaching: Inner vices are intruders in a house that belongs to God; the devotee, unable to evict them alone, hands the problem to the owner with a playful argument that it is the owner's reputation at stake.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Names the seven thieves (ignorance, delusion, greed, ego, pride, anger, lust) who crush him as one without a protector. Reads the close: if they loot your devotee's heart the disgrace is yours, so guard your own house.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same list; quotes a verse attributed to Shankaracharya that lust, anger and greed are thieves living in the body; argues 'bodh-ripu' qualifies Mara (desire), not ignorance.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the heart as Ram's mansion invaded by thieves who trample him as an orphan, ending with his anxiety lest Ram's reputation suffer.

practical_reading: Teachers use the image to externalise anger, greed or compulsions as intruders rather than one's identity, and to ask for help with them instead of fighting alone.
misreadings: Not an excuse ('it's God's problem, not mine'); our existing misuse note already guards this.
Not saying the person is bad: the heart remains the Lord's house even when occupied.
cautions: Being 'trampled as an orphan' with 'no one hearing my cries' may echo real experiences of abuse; keep the reading on inner states.
speaks_to: feeling overrun by anger, greed or craving
shame at what has taken hold of you
feeling outnumbered by your own habits
not_for: someone facing actual intruders or abuse, where the metaphor could minimise real danger

verified_ref: DATA ERROR: this is Vinaya Patrika pada 138, not 128. Haritoshini prints it as (138), Thakur as 138, and in the Gita Press 2001 scan it follows pada 137. (Thakur's pada 128 is a different song, 'O my mind, remember Sita's Lord...'). Our text is stanza 1 and stanza 5 (of 5).
attribution_note: Speaker/listener fine; only the pada number is wrong.
translation_note: Accurate. 'बारक बिबस नाम टेरे' = who called your name even once, helplessly (Poddar/Hari: under compulsion, in distress).
context: A litany of Ram's hand: the hand that made fearless those who called once in distress, broke Shiva's bow and ended Janaka's doubt, lifted the boatman Guha and embraced him like a brother, gave the vulture Jatayu funeral rites and his own abode, killed Bali for Sugriva, crowned the frightened Vibhishana, and freed the gods from fear. Its cool shade removes sin, pain and illusion, and Tulsi longs for it night and day.

key_terms.sense: lotus hand: the blessing, protecting hand
fearlessness, the gesture of 'do not fear'
called the name helplessly, under duress

core_teaching: The hand that protected the frightened and the outcast in the story is the same hand the devotee asks to feel on his own head; its shade cools sin, distress and illusion.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Walks through each deed of the lotus hand (Janaka's doubt, Guha embraced like a brother, Jatayu given rites like a father, Sugriva, Vibhishana, the gods made fearless) and ends with Tulsi wanting its cool, soothing shade day and night.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading, adding that Jatayu was sent to Saketa; notes the pada blends majesty, sweetness, gentleness and parental tenderness.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a plea that the Lord sometime lay on his head the lotus hand that gave refuge to those who called the name once in distress.

practical_reading: Used as a prayer for blessing and reassurance: remembering concrete times protection came, then asking to feel it personally.
misreadings: Not a promise of a physical sign; it is a longing for felt protection.
cautions: Mentions killing Bali and demons in the full pada; the quoted lines are gentle.
speaks_to: longing for a blessing or reassurance
fear and needing to feel protected
wanting the comfort a parent's hand on the head gives
not_for: someone grieving a parent whose blessing they can no longer receive, unless handled gently
research_note: Pada number needs correcting to 138 in our data (id, ref).

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 137, first stanza (of 6) - Gita Press/Poddar 137, Haritoshini 137, Thakur 137.
translation_note: Accurate ('बाँको बार' = to bend a hair, an idiom for the slightest harm).
context: The pada argues from examples that one held by Ram's grace cannot be harmed by enemies: Prahlada, the elephant Gajendra, Vibhishana, Dhruva, Ambarisha (whose curser Durvasa still burns with shame), the Pandavas against Duryodhana. It adds that whoever plots a saint's death dies that death, that he who digs a pit for others falls in it, and that for those who hate saints even the wish-tree bears poison; it ends that one whose helper is Ram is always fearless.

key_terms.sense: a bent hair: the slightest harm

core_teaching: Hostility cannot finally defeat someone held by grace; the devotee need not live in fear of enemies.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: if Ram's grace is there, others' enmity achieves nothing; not a hair of the devotee is bent though one tries crores of ways; whoever plots a saint's death dies by it.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: how can others' enmity touch such a one; even ten million attempts cannot bend a hair on a devotee's head; then the list from Prahlada to Duryodhana's defeat.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to steady fear of opponents or gossip: put trust in grace and right conduct rather than in counter-schemes.
misreadings: Not a promise that nothing bad will ever happen (our misuse note is right).
Not a curse on enemies or a wish for their downfall, although the full pada says plotters fall into their own pits.
cautions: The fuller pada contains retribution lines (the plotter dies the death he planned); avoid them for someone in conflict or wishing harm on others.
For someone who has been harmed, 'not a hair is bent' can imply they lacked grace or faith.
speaks_to: fear of people who wish you harm
workplace or family hostility
feeling targeted
not_for: someone who has already been seriously harmed or abused
someone looking for vindication or revenge
research_note: Viyogi Hari's bhavartha for 137 was not legible in the OCR excerpt; only two sources used.

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 144, first stanza (of 5) - Gita Press/Poddar 144, Haritoshini 144, Thakur 144.
translation_note: Accurate. 'भव-भीर' is the crowd/press of worldly fear (Poddar: fear of birth and death); 'crowd of fears' is fine.
context: The pada lists those Ram saved for the honour of his name: Ajamila, a sinful Brahmin who called his son Narayana at death and was spared Yama's hell; the proud elephant Gajendra, rescued from the crocodile on a single remembrance; the hunter (Valmiki), the boatman Guha, the vulture Jatayu and the courtesan Pingala. It ends with Tulsi asking in what conduct he is worse than they, since he still sinks day and night in a terrible well of darkness.

key_terms.sense: the honour/shame of his own name: Ram protects to keep his name's promise
the press/crowd of worldly fears and troubles

core_teaching: Ram's protection is unconditional and has a long record; that record is the devotee's argument for being saved too.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks who Ram has not kept in his shelter for his name's sake; he is compassionate without cause and removes fear of the round of birth and death.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; stresses that Ajamila was freed even by an accidental 'Narayana', so deliberate remembrance must work too. Notes the pada answers 143's request that Ram camp in Tulsi's heart: how, if the heart is impure? By the name's power.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as: who is there whom you haven't protected for your Name's sake; for no reason you are compassionate and take away the fears of existence.

practical_reading: Used to reassure people who feel too flawed for help: grace is not a reward, and the stories show it reaching the least likely.
misreadings: Not a guarantee of worldly rescue from every crisis.
'Without reason' does not mean arbitrary; it means not conditioned on merit.
cautions: The full pada ends with Tulsi sinking day and night in a dark well; fine as honest lament, but don't end a reading there for someone depressed.
speaks_to: fear that you are beyond help
anxiety with many causes
feeling you have done nothing to deserve kindness
not_for: someone who prayed and was not rescued from a tragedy (the 'who did he not save' framing can wound)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 150, stanzas 1-2 (of 6) - Gita Press/Poddar 150, Haritoshini 150, Thakur 150.
translation_note: Stanza 2 is mistranslated. 'नातो बड़े समर्थ सों इक ओर किधौं हूँ' is a question: is my bond with so great a master one-sided? (Poddar, Viyogi Hari and Thakur all read it so). Our 'On one side is my bond with the great and mighty one, and on the other, I' does not make sense. Suggest: 'Is my bond with one so great and mighty only from my side? You have many like me; I have only you.' Stanza 1 is right: commentators explain he worries because he is still drowning in the world, and doesn't because every soul shares this lot.
context: Tulsi tells Ramabhadra that he both worries and doesn't: all beings suffer, so his lot is common. But is the relationship one-sided? Ram has many like him; he has only Ram. He then admits shame that he is a bad servant who talks like a good one; good or bad, people call him Ram's, and a bad servant, like a bad dog, brings abuse on the master. Seeing no way out of this bind, he asks Ram to do what seems right, look at his list of rescued ones, and not cast off one who has come for refuge.

key_terms.sense: I am anxious, and I am not
vessels of suffering: every embodied being
a one-sided bond (asked as a question)

key_terms.term: तोको मोसे अति घने, मोको एकै तूँ
key_terms.sense: you have so many like me; I have only you

core_teaching: Suffering is common to all, so it need not crush; the real fear is whether the love is returned, and the devotee holds on even if it seems one-sided.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads stanza 1 as: I worry and don't, since all beings are vessels of suffering. Reads stanza 2 as a question: is the bond with a great one only from my side? You have many like me; I only you.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains the worry is that he is still unfreed; the calm is that all beings share it, so he should not fret over karma's fruits.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: troubled and yet not, since all beings are vessels of affliction; is my bond with such a great one only one-sided? Many are close to you, but I have only you.

practical_reading: Speaks to the ache of loving someone or something greater who may not notice you, and to finding calm in the fact that suffering is shared, not personal punishment.
misreadings: Not a statement that God really is indifferent; it is the devotee's fear, voiced honestly.
'All beings suffer' is not meant to dismiss one's own pain.
cautions: 'Every soul is a vessel of suffering' may sound fatalistic to someone in fresh pain.
The 'bad servant like a dog' image later in the pada is harsh self-talk.
speaks_to: feeling your love or devotion is one-sided
feeling like one among many to a teacher, parent or God
anxiety that is also oddly calm
not_for: someone in an unrequited human relationship who may take it as a call to cling
acute grief, if 'everyone suffers' is foregrounded

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 160, refrain and first line (of 3 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 160, Haritoshini 160 (OCR shows '२६०'), Thakur 160.
translation_note: Accurate. 'दोउ बानक बने' = both our roles are set / the pair is complete; 'perfect match' is good.
context: A short pada: the Vedas witness that Ram freed the hunter, the courtesan, the elephant and Ajamila, and countless other low ones; whoever took his name, knowingly or not, was barred from hell. So Tulsi has come for refuge: keep him as your own.

key_terms.sense: the arrangement/pair is made; each role completes the other

core_teaching: A failing is not a disqualification but the very thing that matches the Lord's nature: the fallen and the raiser of the fallen belong together.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I am fallen and you raise the fallen, so our pairing is made and my purification is certain. Notes an old-manuscript variant in stanza 3 ('naraka surapura mane') that he prefers to the common reading.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Says the match is mutual: I needed a raiser of the fallen and you needed someone fallen; both wishes are met. Quotes another devotee's kavitt built on the same pairing of sinner and saviour.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: I'm fallen, you the redeemer, so our roles fit perfectly; whoever took the Name knowingly or unwittingly was shut off from hell and heaven.

practical_reading: Used to turn shame into approach: instead of hiding failure, bring it as the reason to come closer.
misreadings: Not a licence to stay 'fallen' or to keep doing harm because grace will cover it.
cautions: Light and bold in tone; may feel glib to someone carrying serious guilt toward a person they hurt, where repair is also needed.
speaks_to: shame about a failure
feeling unworthy to pray or return
needing a lighter way to approach God
not_for: someone avoiding responsibility toward people they have harmed

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 162, refrain (of 4 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 162, Haritoshini 162, Thakur 162. Sung widely as the bhajan 'Aiso ko udar jag mahin'.
translation_note: Accurate. 'द्रवै' = melts (with pity). 'दीन' could be 'the lowly/helpless' rather than 'the suffering', but either works.
context: The pada proves Ram's generosity by examples: the liberation sages fail to reach through yoga and renunciation he gave to the vulture Jatayu and to Shabari without thinking it much; the wealth Ravana got from Shiva by offering his ten heads Ram gave to Vibhishana, and was even shy about giving it. It ends telling the mind: if you want every happiness, worship Ram, who will fulfil all your desires.

key_terms.sense: generous, magnanimous; Viyogi Hari cites a definition: giving without weighing worthiness, place or time

core_teaching: True generosity gives without waiting for service or merit; Ram's kindness to the lowly is of this kind.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains that only kindness given without return is real; kindness for return is trade. Only God loves without cause.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the refrain as: who in the world is magnanimous like Rama, who melts for the wretched without their serving him; then Jatayu, Shabari and Vibhishana as proofs.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says no one in the world melts at the sight of the lowly without prior service as Ram does.

practical_reading: Teachers use it to describe grace as unearned, and as a model for human giving: help without waiting for the other to have deserved it.
misreadings: Not a promise that worship will deliver every material wish (stanza 4's 'all desires' is devotional hyperbole).
cautions: The closing 'he will fulfil all your desires' can set up disappointment for someone praying for a specific outcome.
speaks_to: feeling you have nothing to offer
receiving unexpected kindness
learning to give without keeping score
not_for: someone bargaining with God for a specific outcome

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 165, stanza 1 and part of stanza 5 (of 5) - Gita Press/Poddar 165, Haritoshini 165, Thakur 165.
translation_note: Accurate. 'गनी' = the rich/those who count themselves important (Poddar widens it to those proud of wealth, learning or rank). Note the pada's final line, which our text omits, ends with a complaint: has no one yet brought poor Tulsi to your notice?
context: Tulsi praises Ram's court for honouring the lowly: the gods, after all their practices, never saw him even in dreams, yet he made brothers of the boatman, bears, monkeys and a demon; he roamed the Dandaka forest with sages but never speaks of it, while he keeps praising Jatayu and Shabari. Stanza 4 cites two Ramayana tales of justice in his kingdom, including keeping in Ayodhya the washerman who slandered Sita. The custom of honouring the poor has always run in this court; only Tulsi seems overlooked.

key_terms.sense: passing over/slighting the rich or self-important
royal court; Ram's kingdom as a court of justice

core_teaching: In Ram's reckoning, humility counts and pride does not: the proud and accomplished are passed over, the humble are embraced.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads 'gani' as those blinded by wealth, learning or rank; Ram honoured the humble boatman, bears and monkeys over the proud gods, praised Jatayu and Shabari over sages, and in Ram-rajya the poor have always been honoured.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: the gods were proud, the bears and monkeys were not; hence the difference in Ram's treatment.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders line 1 differently: Ram disregards honour paid him by the wealthy and gives the poor the fullness of his grace; keeps the ascetic-and-dog and washerman tales and the closing complaint that no one has reminded him of Tulsidasa.

practical_reading: Reassures people who feel unimpressive or overlooked that worth in the spiritual life is not measured by status; also a mirror for anyone who relies on rank.
misreadings: Not an attack on wealthy people as such; the commentators read 'gani' as pride in wealth or status.
cautions: Stanza 4 refers to the washerman who slandered Sita and to Sita's abandonment; do not bring that story into a reading for someone wronged by a partner.
Ends with Tulsi feeling forgotten; don't leave a lonely reader there.
speaks_to: feeling overlooked next to impressive people
low status at work or in family
imposter feelings
not_for: someone wronged by slander in a marriage (stanza 4 can sound like endorsement)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 166, refrain/first stanza of a long pada (Gita Press/Poddar 166, Haritoshini 166 - OCR shows '२६६', Thakur 166).
translation_note: Accurate.
context: The refrain introduces a catalogue of those Ram embraced: Ahalya, turned to stone by her own fault and freed by the touch of his foot; the violent, forest-dwelling Nishada (Guha), hugged without regard to caste; Jayanta, Indra's son, who wronged Sita yet was spared when he finally came for refuge; the meat-eating vulture Jatayu, given funeral rites like a father; Shabari, a woman of low birth outside both custom and Veda; Sugriva; and Vibhishana, the enemy's brother, welcomed with open arms. The pada ends by telling the mind that a life without devotion wastes even one's mother's youth.

key_terms.sense: doing good to others without any motive

core_teaching: Ram's kindness looks for no qualification: caste, species, past wrongdoing or being the enemy's kin do not stop it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Gives the full catalogue: Ahalya freed though without spiritual means, the Nishada embraced without thought of caste, Jayanta sheltered despite his grave offence, Jatayu given a father's rites, Shabari accepted for her love, Sugriva protected, Vibhishana welcomed with outstretched arms.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same catalogue with explanations: Jayanta had pecked Sita's foot as a crow, yet his fear was removed when he came for refuge; Shabari had no standing in society or scripture, yet was given darshan.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the refrain as Rama, the benefactor of the wretched, most tender storehouse of compassion, doing good to others for no reason, then the Ahalya and Nishada stories.

practical_reading: Used to say no one is outside the circle of care, and to challenge readers to extend kindness across caste, class and grudges.
misreadings: Not a statement that the people listed were worthless; the 'low' labels reflect the social view that Ram ignores.
cautions: The fuller pada uses caste and gender language of its time (Shabari as 'low-born, dull woman'); avoid quoting those descriptors.
Jayanta's offence was an assault on Sita; don't use his pardon to counsel a victim to forgive an abuser.
speaks_to: feeling excluded because of background
feeling your past disqualifies you
wanting to practise kindness without conditions
not_for: someone hurt by caste or gender prejudice if the full pada's labels are quoted

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 167, refrain and first line (of 5 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 167, Haritoshini 167, Thakur 167.
translation_note: Accurate. 'जानै सोइ जेहि बनि आई' = only he knows who has managed to do it; 'in whom it has taken root' is a fair paraphrase.
context: After the refrain, Tulsi gives images: whatever skill one has comes easily and gladly to that person, as a small fish swims up the Ganga while a great elephant is swept away; sugar mixed in sand can't be separated by force, yet a tiny ant with a taste for it picks it out. He then describes the state of the yogi who 'sleeps' with the whole world drawn into himself, where grief, delusion, fear, joy, day, night, place and time vanish; until that state, doubt is not uprooted.

key_terms.sense: easy to say, endless to do
has come about/been achieved for someone
the small fish and the elephant: skill beats size

core_teaching: Devotion is easy to describe and hard to live; it is not a matter of strength but of the right 'knack' or taste, which only those who have it truly know.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the images: the little fish swims against the Ganga while the elephant is swept away; sugar in sand can't be separated by force but an ant with the taste gets it easily.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Argues 'Raghupati-bhagati' is one compound, not a vocative; gives as an example of 'easy to say' the Manas description of the saint (contented, without enmity, etc.), which costs the tongue nothing but is hard to live.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as: devotion is hard to perform, simple to tell, and he alone knows who has achieved it; then the fish-and-elephant and ant-and-sugar images.

practical_reading: Honest about the gap between talking about spiritual life and living it; teachers use it to encourage humility and practice over strength or cleverness.
misreadings: Not a claim that devotion is impossible for ordinary people; the fish and ant show the small can succeed where the mighty fail.
Not discouragement from talking about faith, but a warning against confusing talk with practice.
cautions: Could feed discouragement in someone already feeling they fail at faith; pair with the fish/ant images.
speaks_to: frustration that you can't live what you believe
feeling like a hypocrite
being humbled by a practice
not_for: someone who needs reassurance that they are 'doing it right' and will hear only 'it's hard'

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 172, complete in substance (4 stanzas; our text gives stanzas 1-3 and part of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 172, Haritoshini 172, Thakur 172.
translation_note: Accurate. 'नेम' Poddar glosses as the yamas and niyamas; 'my vow' is fine. 'बिगत मान' could also be 'not seeking honour' (Viyogi Hari) as well as 'free of pride'.
context: Tulsi's daydream of a saint's life, asked as a question to himself and Ram: content with whatever comes, wanting nothing from anyone, always at others' service in mind, word and deed; not burning in the fire of harsh words; without pride, calm and cool, speaking of others' virtues, not their faults; dropping the body's worries and bearing joy and sorrow alike. It ends: will Tulsidas, keeping to this path, ever reach unwavering devotion?

key_terms.sense: the same understanding in sorrow and joy

core_teaching: A saint's nature is concrete and ordinary: contentment, service, not reacting to insults, speaking well of others, and steadiness in joy and pain; it is longed for and received by grace, not claimed.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Asks whether by Ram's grace he will ever live with a saint's nature: content with what comes, wanting nothing from men or gods, serving others, keeping the yamas and niyamas; not burning in anger at harsh words.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls this pada the poet's true 'inner kingdom', not fantasy; what the yogi reaches in samadhi the devotee inherits by self-surrender. Glosses 'not burning' as not taking insult and flaring in anger, and 'not speaking faults' as covering others' flaws.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as 'Shall I live such a life some day', listing contentment, doing good, not burning at harsh words, counting virtues not vices, bearing pleasure and pain with equanimity.

practical_reading: Widely used as a checklist for character: when insulted, don't burn; speak of others' good; be content. Framed as a hope, not a standard to beat oneself with.
misreadings: Not a demand to tolerate abuse silently: 'not burning in that fire' is about one's inner anger, not accepting mistreatment.
Not a rejection of ambition or needs; contentment here is freedom from craving.
cautions: Someone in an abusive situation should not be told to 'not burn' at harsh words as if endurance were the goal.
speaks_to: wanting to become a calmer, kinder person
after being insulted or criticised
gossip and fault-finding habits
restlessness and wanting more
not_for: someone currently being verbally abused who needs to set boundaries

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 177, lines 1 and 4 (of 5 short lines) - Gita Press/Poddar 177, Haritoshini 177.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'कुजाचक' = a bad/unworthy beggar (Poddar: a wretched beggar), and 'कुपूत' = an unworthy son; 'poor beggar' slightly softens 'bad beggar'.
context: A five-line vow: even if Ram abandons him, Tulsi will not abandon Ram, for whom else could he love? No master so kind and lovely has been heard of, seen or imagined; Tulsi is a dull soul under maya, Ram the Lord of maya; Tulsi is a bad beggar and unworthy son, Ram the generous giver and caring parent. If anyone else had cared to ask after him, Tulsi says, he would have sold himself to them for nothing.

key_terms.sense: even if you leave me, I won't leave you
unworthy son / mother and father who still wish him well

core_teaching: The devotee's love does not depend on being loved back in a visible way; like a child with parents, the bond holds even when the child is unworthy.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: even if you forsake me I won't leave you, for whose love would I seek leaving your feet? I am the dull jiva under maya, you its Lord.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Adds that there is no other worthy object of love because everything else is impermanent and carries the pain of separation; reads the last line as: had anyone else asked after me, Tulsi would have sold himself for free.

practical_reading: Used to express loyalty in faith during dry periods when God feels absent: 'even if you seem to leave, I stay'.
misreadings: Not a model for staying in a human relationship where one is being abandoned or mistreated.
cautions: 'Bad son' self-description may hurt someone carrying guilt toward their parents; the 'parents' image can sting after a parent's death or estrangement.
speaks_to: feeling abandoned by God or life
staying faithful through a dry season
feeling unworthy yet loved
not_for: someone being abandoned by a partner, if read as 'stay no matter what'
research_note: Thakur's rendering not checked for this pada.

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 179, stanzas 1-2 (of 5) - Gita Press/Poddar 179, Haritoshini 179 (OCR '१७६'), Thakur 179.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'अंगहीन' = one with no limbs/means, i.e. utterly without support or resources (Poddar: without spiritual means; Viyogi Hari: helpless, with no shelter). 'जग जगदीस घर घरनि घनेरे हैं' both commentators read sardonically: in every house there are plenty of self-styled 'lords of the world'; our 'would-be lords' captures it.
context: Tulsi asks where he can go and whom he can tell; for one without any means, Ram alone is the way in the three worlds. Plenty of people play lord, but only Ram's qualities support the supportless. Who else ran to save the elephant, leaving even Garuda behind? Who else made a coward and worthless son like Tulsi precious? Tulsi's spoiled affairs will come right only if Ram makes them; delay will only breed more fault and sorrow.
core_teaching: When there is no one to tell and no means left, there is still a refuge whose very nature is to support those who have none.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it as: where shall I go, who will hear one without spiritual means; for such a one you alone are the refuge in three worlds.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Glosses 'anghin' as helpless with no shelter; says everyone in the world claims to be the master of all, but the supportless cross only by singing Ram's qualities.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening as: where shall I go, whom shall I tell, who will listen to this wretched one; in three worlds you are the only way for those without means.

practical_reading: For moments of having no one to talk to: the act of speaking the trouble to God is itself the first support.
misreadings: Not a claim that human help is worthless; it mocks self-important 'lords', not friends or helpers.
cautions: A reader who truly has no one may need a pointer to human support too; the verse can deepen isolation if read alone.
The full pada calls Tulsi a coward and worthless son.
speaks_to: having no one to tell
feeling helpless and without resources
being let down by powerful people
not_for: someone in a crisis who needs a helpline or a person, if used as a substitute

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 181, stanzas 1 and 4 (of 5) - Gita Press/Poddar 181, Haritoshini 181, Thakur 181.
translation_note: Accurate in sense. Literally 'करम-कपीस बालि-बली' = karma, the mighty monkey-king Bali: crooked karma is cast as Bali and Tulsi as the terrified Sugriva (Poddar, Viyogi Hari).
context: Tulsi asks Ram to look his way by any means; he has no other place. His mind is harder than a thousand stones (who else freed a stone, Ahalya?); he wants to perform a sacrifice of love at Ram's feet like Vishvamitra, but fears the demons of the age; he fears his crooked karma as Sugriva feared Bali and wants to live under Ram's arm; delusion strikes him as Ravana struck Vibhishana, and he burns in the three fires of suffering. Each stanza borrows a Ramayana rescue.

key_terms.sense: karma as the mighty monkey-king Bali
to live in the shelter of your arm

core_teaching: The devotee maps his inner struggles onto Ram's past rescues: as Ram protected Sugriva from Bali, he can protect one hunted by his own past deeds.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Takes each stanza as a parallel: free my stone-like mind as you freed Ahalya; guard my sacrifice of love as you guarded Vishvamitra's from demons.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: let me live in the shadow of your arm and save me from crooked deeds; explains 'three fires' as bodily, worldly and divine afflictions.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: I am terrified by the terrors of karma like Sugriva by the mighty Vanara-chief Bali; Lord of those without a lord, I long to dwell in the shelter of your arms.

practical_reading: Helps someone haunted by the consequences of past actions to ask for protection and a place to stand while they face them.
misreadings: Not a way to escape consequences of one's actions; it asks for shelter while facing them.
cautions: Being 'hunted' by karma could feed guilt in someone already self-blaming.
speaks_to: fear of past mistakes catching up
feeling hunted or pursued
needing a protector
not_for: someone in real physical danger from a person, where the metaphor might replace practical safety steps

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 182, stanzas 4-5 (of 7) - Gita Press/Poddar 182, Haritoshini 182, Thakur 182.
translation_note: Accurate. 'बाप! बलि जाउँ' = 'Father, I offer myself / may I be your sacrifice'; 'आप करिये उपाउ सो' = you devise some such remedy. 'हारेहू सुदाउ' = even after losing, a good throw (dice image).
context: Tulsi says hearing Ram's qualities fills him with longing, but he doesn't know the devotion that pleases Ram: his deeds, nature and times are bad, he has no master, home, wealth, health, steady mind or long life. Whoever he asks for water asks him for nectar instead, so he dares not speak to anyone. So he asks his 'father' to devise the remedy: Ram's glance turns a losing throw into a winning one, makes the unseen seen and the incomprehensible understood. He ends saying he lives in the water of Ram's name like a big fish, and has at least reported his own conduct honestly to his master.

key_terms.sense: I offer myself to you; an expression of devotion
a winning throw even after losing (dice)
showing the unseeable, explaining the incomprehensible

core_teaching: When one has no qualifications and no ideas left, one can hand the problem over: a single glance of grace can reverse a losing position and bring clarity.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Lists what Tulsi lacks (good deeds, nature, times, master, home, wealth, body, mind, long life); those he asks for water demand nectar; so, father, you devise the remedy, for your glance turns defeat into a good throw.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; in a note sums up Tulsi's plight as bad deeds, low nature, the Kali age, no protector, poverty, lifelong illness and a restless mind, and asks what cure there can be.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: O my father, as I offer myself, do something for me; by your glance even in defeat comes a winning stake.

practical_reading: For when you've run out of plans: admit it, hand it over, and stay open to seeing what you couldn't see before.
misreadings: Not a promise of a specific outcome (our misuse note is right).
Not a reason to stop seeking practical, medical, legal or emotional help.
cautions: Gambling/dice image ('losing throw') - avoid for readers struggling with gambling.
speaks_to: feeling out of options
not knowing the right way to pray
after a loss or defeat
confusion about what to do next
not_for: someone with a gambling problem
someone awaiting a medical or legal result, if read as a guarantee

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 183, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 183, Haritoshini 183, Thakur 183.
translation_note: Accurate. Poddar glosses 'बड़े की बड़ाई' as the pride of the great and 'छोटे की छोटाई' as the lowliness/wretchedness of the small: love removes both.
context: Tulsi praises Ram as the one who knows the ways of love: the Vedas honour him for removing the pride of the great and the lowliness of the small. He performed the vulture's funeral rites and ate the Bhil woman Shabari's fruits; whoever he honours is honoured by the world and the Veda, and his love is reckoned weightier than yoga or knowledge. Tulsi, though dry of love and in others' control, sits stubbornly at the door of the friend of the poor.

key_terms.sense: the litany of one's famed titles

core_teaching: Love levels: it humbles the proud and raises the lowly, so that both meet as equals.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains the Vedas praise Ram for removing the great one's pride and the small one's lowliness; he did Jatayu's rites and ate Shabari's fruits; whom he honours, world and Veda honour; his love outweighs yoga and knowledge.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads 'badai' as the arrogance of the proud and 'chhotai' as the smallness of the small, both removed by Ram's love.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: you know well the ways of love; you do away with the greatness of the great and the smallness of the small.

practical_reading: Used to describe how real love works in families and communities: it neither flatters status nor lets anyone feel small.
misreadings: Not a call to erase all distinctions or roles; it is about pride and shame melting in love.
speaks_to: feeling small or inferior
feeling superior and wanting to let it go
relationships with a big status gap

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 184, opening line (of 5 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 184, Haritoshini 184, Thakur 184.
translation_note: Accurate. 'जियकी जरनि' = the burning of the heart/mind (Viyogi Hari: the mind becomes calm).
context: The first line is the refrain of a pada on the name in the Kali age: other means have become as useless as a painted sun for dispelling darkness; rituals are mixed with sin like trees that flower without fruit; worship is ruined by hypocrisy and greed, knowledge has become a way to fill the belly; yoga, renunciation and wisdom are mostly talk and costume. Shiva teaches the name to the dying at Kashi. Tulsi ends: keep the mind, love and refuge in Ram's name alone, and Ram will one day pour out his kindness.

key_terms.sense: the burning of the heart: anguish, agitation
a painted sun: a remedy that looks real but cannot work

core_teaching: Repeating Ram's name cools the inner burning when elaborate methods have become hollow.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Says the heart's burning goes only by japa of Ram's name; other means in Kali are like a painted sun against darkness; rituals, worship and knowledge have decayed into show and livelihood; Shiva at Kashi teaches the name's power.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Glosses: the mind will be calmed only by japa of the name; other means look easy but fail midway, like trees with lovely flowers and useless fruit.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: by the repetition of Rama's Name the burning of the heart is banished; in Kali other means are as futile as a painting of the sun to dispel darkness.

practical_reading: Teachers use it as a simple practice for agitation: repeat the name slowly when the mind is on fire.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of all other spiritual practices or of therapy; the critique is of hollow, show-based practice.
Not instant relief; the closing stanza speaks of steady trust over time.
cautions: The fuller pada criticises religious hypocrisy broadly; avoid using it to belittle others' practice.
speaks_to: anger or anxiety that burns
exhaustion with complicated practices
needing something simple to hold on to
not_for: someone with a medical cause of agitation, if offered as a replacement for care

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 189, stanza 1 and a later stanza (of 5) - Gita Press/Poddar 189, Haritoshini 189 (OCR '१८६'), Thakur 189.
translation_note: Accurate. 'भव-बेगारि' = the forced, unpaid labour of worldly existence (Poddar: the round of birth and death; Viyogi Hari: Yama's messengers can't press a Ram-chanter into it). 'नाउँ गाउँ कर भूला' = forgot the name of the village, i.e. lost sight of home/destination.
context: A walking song in folk idiom. Keep saying Ram as you go, or you'll be seized for the world's forced labour. Crooked karma has handed us, free of charge, a rickety three-cornered litter (the body) with old bamboo and a mismatched frame; its five bearers (the senses) are drunk with desire and stagger, so the rider gets jolted. The road is thorny, there are no provisions, and the traveller has forgotten the name of his village; Tulsi asks Ram to be kind and remove the fear of the world.

key_terms.sense: forced labour of worldly existence / rebirth
forgot the name of one's village: lost one's true home or goal

core_teaching: Life is a hard journey in an unreliable vehicle with unruly senses; keeping the name on one's lips is the way to keep walking and not be conscripted into endless drudgery.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: keep saying Ram or you'll be caught in the world's forced labour, from which escape is very hard.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Works out the allegory in detail: karma the carpenter gave the body free; the old bamboo is age-old craving; the three corners are waking, dream and deep sleep.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders it as a marching refrain, 'Go onward saying Rama', with the rotten three-cornered cot of the body carried by bearers drunk with lust, on a road full of thorns.

practical_reading: Used as a mantra for hard stretches: when you feel lost, tired and unprovisioned, keep putting one foot in front of the other with the name.
misreadings: Not contempt for the body; the litter image is about not mistaking the vehicle for the destination.
Not a prediction of doom for those who don't chant.
cautions: Rebirth/'forced labour' framing could feel threatening; keep the tone of the refrain, which is companionable ('brother').
speaks_to: feeling lost or having forgotten what you're working toward
a long hard stretch of life
being pulled in many directions by cravings
not_for: someone with a chronic illness or disability, if the 'rotten body' allegory is emphasised

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 201, refrain (of 5 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 201, Haritoshini 201, Thakur 201.
translation_note: Accurate. 'घटत न काज पराये' = never comes to be of use in another's work (Poddar: never came of use to others).
context: Tulsi addresses his own mind: what was gained by a human birth if it never, even in a dream, served others in body, word or mind? The pleasures you chase come unbidden in heaven or hell, at home or in the forest, yet you struggle for them; under delusion you pursued others' wives and enmity and forgot the suffering of the womb; fear, sleep, sex and food are shared by every creature, so a body rare even for gods was wasted in pride. If the sense of 'mine and yours' never left and the mind never settled in Ram, what use is regret once the chance has passed?

key_terms.sense: the human body/birth, prized as rare
the sense of 'mine' versus 'others'' (later in the pada)

core_teaching: Human life is distinguished from animal life by service and devotion; a life that never helps another has missed its point.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads it: what gain from a human body if it never served others in mind, speech or body; sense-pleasure comes unasked anywhere, yet the mind toils for it; eating, sleeping, fear and mating are common to all beings.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Gives the same bhavartha and glosses 'nij-par-buddhi' as the division between one's own and others'. (The preceding pada 200 in the same commentary uses Kabir sakhis on death to the same end.)

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: what gain being born into this human life when even in a dream you never served in the affairs of others, in speech, thought and deed.

practical_reading: A plain prompt for today: do one useful thing for someone else, in deed, word or thought.
misreadings: Not a judgment that people who are unwell or unable to help others have wasted their lives.
cautions: The full pada mentions adultery, enmity and the 'suffering in the womb'; keep to the refrain for general readers.
Could induce guilt in someone depressed and unable to function; frame as invitation, not verdict.
speaks_to: feeling life lacks purpose
self-absorption or loneliness
wanting to start serving others
not_for: someone bedridden, depressed or burned out by caregiving, who may hear it as accusation

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 217, stanza 1 and stanza 6 (of 6) - Gita Press/Poddar 217, Haritoshini 217, Thakur 217.
translation_note: Accurate. 'आपसे कहुँ सौंपिये मोहि' = hand me over to someone like yourself (both commentators note that is impossible, which is the point).
context: Tulsi explains why he keeps weeping before Ram: if there were anyone else, he would go there. Who else loves the poor, bears the name 'purifier of the fallen', gave Ajamila his abode? Shiva, Brahma, Indra and the guardians were there, but none helped the drowning elephant; in an assembly of capable kings, none clothed Draupadi when she cried out. If Ram is disgusted with him, let him hand Tulsi to someone like himself; otherwise how could Tulsi leave his feet?
core_teaching: Repeated crying to God is not nagging but the natural result of having no one else who truly helps; the devotee even dares God to find a substitute.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: if there were another refuge I would not keep troubling you with my sorrows; none but you loves the lowly; no god helped the elephant, no capable king clothed Draupadi.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading: he would rather not trouble Ram but finds no one else who removes the pain of the poor.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: if only there were any other, O Lord, why should I time on time tell weeping my long tale of woes to you?

practical_reading: Gives permission to keep bringing the same sorrow in prayer, again and again, without shame.
misreadings: Not a statement that people around us are useless; it contrasts human limits with divine help.
cautions: Stanza 4 recalls Draupadi's public humiliation; avoid it for readers who have experienced sexual violence.
'If you find me distasteful' may echo a reader's fear of being a burden; reassure.
speaks_to: feeling you keep bringing the same pain
fear of being a burden
no one else to turn to
not_for: survivors of sexual assault (Draupadi stanza)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 221, stanza 1 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 221, Haritoshini 221, Thakur 221 (number confirmed in GP and Haritoshini).
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Tulsi says he watches day and night for the road by which grace will come, not knowing when. Virtues, knowledge, renunciation and devotion fled in panic at the sight of the Kali age, leaving a store of sins; injustice has made the earth hotter than the sun; he has no other place and his mind is distraught; no one, not even his own body, is his. He ends with a monsoon image: Tulsi is a ripening paddy field drying up, so Ram, dark as a rain cloud, should become the cloud and water it.

key_terms.sense: watching only the road of grace
dark as a rain-cloud: Ram as the cloud that can water the drying field (stanza 4)

core_teaching: Waiting for grace without knowing when it will come is itself a form of devotion; the devotee keeps watching the road.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I, a poor one, keep watching for your grace day and night; when it will come cannot be known; virtues and spiritual means fled before the Kali age; the earth burns hotter than the sun with injustice.

practical_reading: For long waits (for healing, news, a turn in life): keep watching the road, without pretending to know the date.
misreadings: Not passivity: waiting here is attentive and expectant.
cautions: Describes a world of injustice and decay; can feel bleak. Lead with the waiting and the rain-cloud ending.
speaks_to: a long waiting period
drought of feeling or faith
not knowing when things will change
not_for: someone in an urgent situation who needs action now
research_note: Haritoshini prints this as pada 221 (text and number checked) but its bhavartha was illegible in the OCR excerpt; Thakur not checked. Only one commentary (Poddar).

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 226, stanzas 1 and 5 (of 6) - Gita Press/Poddar 226, Haritoshini 226, Thakur 226.
translation_note: Accurate. 'हौं सिसु-अरनि अरो' = I, like a child, have dug in stubbornly (Viyogi Hari: I am pestering/insisting with a child's obstinacy before these two letters). 'दोउ आखर' = the two syllables Ra-ma.
context: Tulsi says: let others rely on what they rely on; for him Ram's name is the wish-tree fruiting with welfare in this age. Karma, worship, knowledge and Vedic doctrine are all true, but like someone who went blind in the monsoon month and sees only green, he sees only the name. He licked leaf-plates like a dog and never filled his belly; now remembering the name he finds nectar served. Where one's love and trust are, there one's work is accomplished; the two syllables are his parents and he sits stubborn as a child before them. He swears, with Shiva as witness, he is not inventing this.

key_terms.sense: like one blinded in the monsoon month who sees only green everywhere
dug in like an obstinate child

core_teaching: Tulsi does not dismiss other paths; he simply testifies that for him the name has done everything, and that results follow where one's love and trust are.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: whoever relies on another may do so; for me the name is the wish-tree of welfare in Kali. Karma, worship and knowledge are all true, but like one blinded in Shravan I see only the name.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Stresses Tulsi grants the other paths are genuine; he simply sees only the name. Explains the Shravan-blind image, and reads the last stanza: work succeeds where love and trust are.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: let him put his trust elsewhere who will; for me the wishing-tree of Rama's Name has borne fruit even in Kali; karma, knowledge and worship are still good, but like one gone blind in Shravana I see only green.

practical_reading: A model for personal faith without judging others: say what has worked for you and trust it wholeheartedly.
misreadings: Not a claim that other paths are false; both commentators note Tulsi calls them true.
Not a guarantee that any wish will be granted.
cautions: Image of licking leaf-plates like a dog may evoke real poverty and shame.
speaks_to: finding one simple practice that works for you
after many attempts that never satisfied
being judged for your way of faith
not_for: interfaith settings if read as 'only this works'

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 227, stanzas 1 and 3 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 227, Haritoshini 227, Thakur 227.
translation_note: Stanza 3's last line is slightly off. 'नाम-प्रसाद लहत रसाल-फल अब हौं बबुर बहेरे' = by the name's grace I now get mangoes from babul and bahera trees (Poddar, Viyogi Hari, Thakur): the same thorny trees that gave nothing now yield mangoes (Viyogi Hari: people who once scorned me now honour me). Our translation makes Tulsi himself the babul ('I who was a thorny babul now get mangoes'), and our line says 'I now bear sweet fruit'. Suggest: 'By the name's grace I now get mangoes from babul and bahera trees.' The note's 'babul and bahera' is right. Also stanza 2 (omitted) states his parents abandoned him at birth, which supports the setting.
context: Tulsi proclaims, arms raised, to all companions in worldly and spiritual life that Ram's name alone is his well-wisher. His mother and father abandoned him at birth and fate made him luckless and odd, yet some now call him 'Ram's own' - only because of the name. Without the name he wandered craving food, so pitiable that sorrow itself grieved; now the thorny trees give him mangoes. Saints build both worlds by study and many practices; Tulsi has only the name, the one knot under many windings.

key_terms.sense: with arms raised: a public declaration
thorny babul and bitter bahera trees / mango

core_teaching: Out of abandonment and hunger, the name turned a barren life into a fruitful one: the world that gave thorns now gives sweetness.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I declare to companions in this world and the next that your name alone does me good; parents left me at birth and fate made me unlucky.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading, glossing the trees as people who once slighted him now honouring him; notes the legend that Tulsi's parents abandoned him because of an inauspicious horoscope, adding that no old astrology text prescribes this.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: my parents abandoned me at birth; without the Name I wandered craving for my stomach's sake and even Sorrow grew sad; now by the Name's grace I get mango fruits from the babul and bahera trees.

practical_reading: Speaks to anyone who began life with very little: what once gave only thorns can, with grace and steadiness, become a source of sweetness.
misreadings: Not a promise of material prosperity through chanting.
cautions: Explicitly about parental abandonment at birth and childhood hunger; may be raw for adoptees or people abandoned by parents. Handle gently.
speaks_to: a hard or abandoned childhood
coming up from poverty
being looked down on and now respected
gratitude after hardship
not_for: someone currently in hunger or homelessness who needs practical help, if read as 'just chant'

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 229, stanzas 1 and 3 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 229, Haritoshini 229 (OCR '२९९'), Thakur 229.
translation_note: Accurate. 'तिहारेहि कौर को' = (lived) on your morsel/scraps (Viyogi Hari: on your leftovers, i.e. always your servant). 'बड़े ठेकाने ठौर को' = belonging to a great establishment (Poddar: a servant of Ram's royal court).
context: Tulsi swears his tongue would rot if he called himself anyone else's: birth after birth he has lived on Ram's food. In three worlds and three times he sees no friend equal to Ram, and if he deceives Ram may he be a worm in hell for aeons. Even if the age has made his mind a whirligig beetle on the water, it skims the surface and does not sink; Tulsi stays cool and calm because he belongs to a great house.

key_terms.sense: a morsel of food: livelihood from the master's table

core_teaching: Security comes from knowing whose you are: one who belongs to a great house stays calm even when the times toss the mind about.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: may my tongue rot if I call myself another's; birth after birth I have lived on your food; no friend like you anywhere; though Kali has made my mind a whirligig in the river, it will float, not drown.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that the whirligig skims the water without sinking, so the world can't master him.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
