commentaries.gist: Renders: may my tongue melt if I say I belong to another master; I have lived off the scraps of your food; Tulsidasa is ever calm by this strength, that he is at a great good place.

practical_reading: Helps someone steady their identity in unsettled times: the mind may be tossed, but knowing where you belong keeps you afloat.
misreadings: Not a call to swear oaths or curse oneself.
Not servility toward human masters.
cautions: Contains a self-curse (a worm in hell for aeons if deceitful) in stanza 2; omit for anxious or scrupulous readers.
speaks_to: anxiety in turbulent times
needing a sense of belonging
feeling tossed about but wanting to stay calm
not_for: readers with religious scrupulosity or OCD (oath and hell imagery)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 232, stanza 1 (of 4) - Haritoshini 232, Thakur 232. (The pada could not be located in the Gita Press 2001 OCR text; it appears in that edition's index as 232.)
translation_note: Accurate. 'पर-पीर पाइहै' = will understand/feel another's pain (Viyogi Hari glosses 'paihai' as 'will understand').
context: Tulsi asks where he would find another friend of the poor: who else understands another's pain, to whom else could he tell his wretchedness? Wherever he turns his mind he finds masters either without compassion or kind but incapable, so he keeps silent rather than expose himself for nothing. He admits his deeds would drown him in a cow's hoofprint while his talk plumbs the ocean; inwardly greedy and a servant of desire, outwardly he calls himself Ram's. Ram knows his heart anyway; he asks to be helped to sing Ram's praise without deceit.

key_terms.sense: friend/kinsman of the poor and helpless
(later) drowning in a cow's hoofprint while talking of the ocean: deeds small, words big

core_teaching: Real help needs both compassion and capacity; finding that only in God, the devotee brings his sorrow there and admits his own gap between words and deeds.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains: no one but Ram does good to others, understands others' pain or consoles; masters are either merciless or merciful but incapable, so I stay silent rather than reveal my secret for nothing; my deeds are tiny, my talk vast.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: where else shall I find another friend of the poor; who besides you would feel another's sorrow; I see lords without compassion, or compassionate but unworthy, so I keep silent.

practical_reading: For those who have stopped telling people their troubles: it names why (no one both cares and can help) and opens a place to speak.
misreadings: Not advice to stop confiding in people; it is about where ultimate refuge lies.
cautions: Could reinforce someone's isolation ('no one else understands'); pair with encouragement toward trusted people.
speaks_to: feeling no one understands your pain
keeping silent about troubles
hypocrisy you notice in yourself
not_for: someone withdrawing from all human support in depression
research_note: Gita Press 2001 OCR text for 232 not located; two sources used.

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 240, stanzas 1 and 4 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 240, Haritoshini 240, Thakur 240.
translation_note: Mostly accurate. 'लै कासी प्रयाग कब सीझे' - both commentators read 'कासी' as a variant of 'करसी' (dung-cake fire): when did they burn themselves in the five-fire austerity at Prayag? Viyogi Hari prints 'करसी' with 'कासी' as a variant. Our 'made perfect by Kashi or Prayag' follows the 'Kashi' reading; acceptable, but the sense is 'when did they perform harsh austerities at holy places'. 'जल की चिकनाई' = the slickness water leaves on the skin, which vanishes when dry (Poddar): 'oil on water' changes the image; better 'like the sheen water leaves, gone when it dries'.
context: Tulsi argues that goodness is whatever pleases Ram, not ritual standing: the courtesan Pingala, the vulture Jatayu and the hunter Valmiki reached Hari's abode without austerities at holy places; King Nriga never left the Vedic path yet suffered for ages as a lizard; the elephant had no initiation yet Ram rushed to him. Ram left high-born gods, sages and Brahmins to be born in a cowherd's house, refused Duryodhana's wealth and ate at humble Vidura's. Ram is won by simple, natural love; everything else is like the wet sheen of water that dries away.

key_terms.sense: the slickness water leaves, which vanishes as it dries: impressive but impermanent

core_teaching: Virtue is measured by Ram's pleasure, and he is won by simple, sincere love rather than ritual rank, austerity or status.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: whomever you are pleased with is the truly virtuous; Pingala, Jatayu and Valmiki reached your abode without burning in dung-fire austerities at Prayag; Nriga kept the Vedic path yet suffered; Ram chose a cowherd's home and Vidura's food.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; prints 'karasi' (dung-cake) with 'Kashi' as a variant; glosses 'dichhit' as an initiated sacrificer; says Ram is subject to guileless love and not won by other means.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: whoever you are pleased with is truly pure; the prostitute, vulture and hunter were taken to the Lord's abode, but when did they burn in Kasi and Prayaga?

practical_reading: Reassures people who feel spiritually 'unqualified' (no rituals, pilgrimages, learning) that sincere love counts most.
misreadings: Not a rejection of all practice or pilgrimage; it says these don't substitute for love.
Not an endorsement of the 'courtesan' label as a moral judgment.
cautions: Nriga's story (a righteous king suffering) could unsettle someone who suffers despite doing right; use carefully.
speaks_to: feeling you lack the right rituals, learning or background
doubting your worth in a religious community
wanting a simpler faith
not_for: someone devoted to pilgrimage or ritual who may hear it as dismissive

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 250, final stanza (stanza 4 of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 250, Haritoshini 250, Thakur 250.
translation_note: Accurate. 'कहरु' = cruelty/havoc (Viyogi Hari: injustice). 'हारि हिये न हहरु' = don't lose heart and tremble.
context: Tulsi says if he had any other master or place he wouldn't keep pestering Ram; Ram has raised lazy, unlucky ones like him, so Ram is his king and Ayodhya his city. He has not served other deities; the name alone is his welfare, vow and love, his nectar, while other supports are poison. Thieves and watchmen (vices and virtues) are all in Ram's hands, and Ram never delays in helping the suffering, so why delay for him? The ending (our lines): trusting Ram's ways yet frightened by the age's havoc, he asks Ram to say, or have someone say, 'Tulsi, you are mine; don't lose heart.'

key_terms.sense: it will be well only if you say it, or have it said

core_teaching: Faith and fear can coexist; what calms the fear is hearing, directly or through someone else, the word of belonging: 'you are mine, don't be afraid'.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains he would not keep calling if he had another master; Ram raised the lazy and unlucky, so Ram is his king; the name is his welfare and the rest is poison; vices and virtues are both in Ram's hand.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; glosses 'kaharu' as injustice and 'jog-chhem' as gaining and keeping; says it is up to Ram whether the thieves (lust, anger) loot him or the watchmen (discernment, dispassion) guard him.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the opening: had there been any other master or place of rest I wouldn't have pestered the Lord again and again; you're my king and Avadha my city.

practical_reading: In frightening times, it helps to ask for and receive reassurance, even through another person's voice ('have it said'): a friend, teacher or scripture can carry the words 'you are held'.
misreadings: Not a claim that fear means lack of faith; both are present.
cautions: Stanza 2 says he serves no other deity and calls other supports poison; avoid it for mixed-faith readers.
'These times' language can amplify anxiety about the world; keep the focus on the reassurance.
speaks_to: fear about the state of the world
anxiety despite faith
needing to hear 'you are mine, don't be afraid'
not_for: readers from other traditions if stanza 2 is used

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 253, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 253, Haritoshini 253, Thakur 253.
translation_note: Accurate. 'आरत-प्रनत-पाल' = protector of the afflicted and those who bow/surrender.
context: Tulsi asks to be kept in Ram's shelter as Ram has kept such people always; no one so kind is known in three worlds and three times. Ram has raised the lazy, unlucky and sinful, and still feels he hasn't repaid the orphans; Ram is capable, and Tulsi, such as he is, is Ram's. Disgusted and frightened by the ways of the age, he asks Ram to say just once, smiling or frowning, 'Tulsi, you are mine'; he swears that this alone would uproot all his sorrow.

key_terms.sense: as you have kept (me/such ones) all along
protector of the suffering who bow to him

core_teaching: The best argument for future care is past care: as you have kept me until now, keep me still.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: keep me in your shelter, as you have always taken in people like me; none so kind in three worlds and times; you raised the lazy and sinful and still felt in debt to orphans.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; worries that the age may turn his mind from Ram's feet; quotes Vyasa's lament on the Kali age and a Bhagavata verse that the heart's knot breaks on seeing the Lord.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: O Rama, take me under your refuge as you have ever done; no other is known to be so merciful; I'm yours however I may be.

practical_reading: Encourages a reader to remember the times they were carried through, and to let that memory ground trust for what's next.
misreadings: Not a claim that suffering will stop because one has been protected before.
speaks_to: uncertainty about the future
wanting continuity of care
looking back on having been held
not_for: someone who feels they have never been kept or protected (the premise may ring false)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 254, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 254, Haritoshini 254, Thakur 254.
attribution_note: Setting ('orphaned as a child') is biographical framing from pada 227 and tradition, not stated in this pada. Acceptable as context but should not be presented as what this verse says.
translation_note: Accurate. 'सुहृद' = a friend who wishes well without motive (Poddar: an unconditional well-wisher). 'प्रेम-पन' = vow/pledge of love.
context: Tulsi says Ram's name is his mother and father, kin, beloved, teacher, master, companion and true friend, and his firm love for it is his unshakeable wealth. Shiva churned the vast curd-ocean of a hundred crore Ram-stories and drew out the name as butter; trust in the name is the fruit of all four goals of life; it serves both worldly and spiritual ends, and nothing does as much good.
core_teaching: Every relationship one needs can be found in the name; love for it is a wealth that does not diminish.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: your name is my parents, kin, lover, guru, master, friend and selfless well-wisher; my single love for it is my unshakeable wealth; Shiva churned the name like ghee from the curd-ocean of countless stories.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; adds that ordinary wealth shrinks when spent while the name-wealth grows daily and is inexhaustible.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders the name as mother, father, kin, lover, teacher, lord, friend and companion, and the vow of love for it as his enduring wealth; Shiva churned his countless deeds to extract the name like ghee.

practical_reading: For someone missing family or mentors, the name (or practice) can become a steady relationship that holds all these roles.
misreadings: Not a call to abandon or replace human family and friends.
cautions: Mention of mother and father may be tender for the bereaved or estranged; the verse can comfort but should be offered gently.
speaks_to: loneliness
loss of parents or mentors
wanting something that doesn't run out
not_for: someone in fresh grief for a parent, if framed as replacement

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 257, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 257, Haritoshini 257, Thakur 257.
translation_note: Second line is slightly misread. 'आपको भले हैं सब, आपनेको कोऊ कहूँ' = everyone is good to themselves (seeks their own good), and only someone, somewhere, is good to their own dependants (Poddar, Viyogi Hari, Thakur all read it so). Our 'Everyone is good to their own people, and someone somewhere is good to their own' blurs the contrast. Suggest: 'Everyone looks after themselves; only a rare one looks after their own people; but your feet, Ram, do good to all.'
context: Tulsi warns that if the friend of the poor pushes the poor away, they have nowhere else. Most people seek their own good, a rare one cares for his dependants, but Ram's feet do good to everyone. He turned glass into gold: the stone (Ahalya), beasts, a bird, Kol and Bhil forest-dwellers and a demon; the Dandaka forest grew holy at his touch and withered trees bloomed. His name helps even those turned against him; no one else destroys sorrow and fault, and one can say anything to so gentle a master.

key_terms.sense: good to oneself / good to one's own
your feet are good to all

core_teaching: Most care is self-interested or limited to one's own circle; divine care extends to everyone, which is why the helpless can rely on it.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: if you remove this poor one he has no other refuge; nearly everyone wants their own good, few do good to their servants; your feet do good to all, good and bad alike.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading ('one in a lakh' cares for dependants); adds that the name helps both the hostile and the devoted; quotes a Rahim doha about being drawn close and then flung away like an arrow, which Tulsi fears.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: if you turn away from this wretch he has no other refuge; all seek their own good, but rarely one who seeks the good of his servants; your feet are good for all.

practical_reading: Challenges readers to widen their care beyond themselves and their own circle, and comforts those who have no circle.
misreadings: Not cynicism about all people; it contrasts ordinary limited care with universal care.
cautions: Fear of being pushed away may echo rejection by family; reassure.
speaks_to: fear of rejection
having no one of your own
wanting to care beyond your circle

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 261, first line (of 4 stanzas) - Gita Press/Poddar 261, Haritoshini 261, Thakur 261.
translation_note: Accurate. 'पल पाउ' = a quarter of a moment. Poddar reads 'मेरी' as 'my good destiny/salvation'; Viyogi Hari as 'my doing/affairs'; our 'what I try to make of myself' is a fair middle.
context: Tulsi confesses: what he tries to fix would not come right in millions of aeons, but Ram can fix it in a quarter-moment. He traded the priceless jewel of life for wild berries; his mind is dirty, his tongue babbled instead of repeating the name, he took wrong roads and never did good even by mistake; any good deed done by imitation or company he advertised, and he hid his sins, feeding attachment, hatred and anger. Yet the world says Tulsi trusts and loves Ram, and his real support is Ram.

key_terms.sense: (stanza 1) exchanged the priceless jewel of life for berries

core_teaching: Self-repair by one's own power is endless; grace can accomplish in a moment what effort alone never finishes.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: my salvation by my own means won't come in crores of kalpas, but if you wish it, it comes in a quarter moment; I traded life's jewel for the berries of sense pleasure.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; says he wasted life on sense objects and never worshipped; concludes that past, present and future show he has done no good, yet the world says Tulsi belongs to Ram and he trusts Ram.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: by my own efforts it won't be done in a million aeons, but by you it will be achieved in the quarter of a wink; I took mere ber-fruits in exchange for life's priceless jewel.

practical_reading: Releases perfectionists from the belief that everything depends on their own effort, while still naming honestly what went wrong.
misreadings: Not a reason to stop trying (our misuse note is right).
Not a claim that one's life has been worthless; it is a devotional confession.
cautions: The full pada is harsh self-accusation (never did good even by mistake); avoid quoting it to someone with low self-worth.
speaks_to: exhaustion from trying to fix yourself
perfectionism
feeling stuck despite effort
not_for: someone with severe self-criticism or depression, if the confession stanzas are used

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 266, stanza 1 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 266, Haritoshini 266, Thakur 266.
translation_note: Accurate. 'चहुँ जुग रस एक' = of one unchanging nature in all four ages.
context: Tulsi admits the harder he tries to come near, the further he falls; Ram is the same in every age, and Tulsi is still his despite his faults. Finding him separated, the vile age tricked him: turned gold to base metal, a king to a beggar, a good mind to a bad one; he wandered countless hills and forests burning without fire. Only when he went to Chitrakut did he see through the age's tricks, and now he fears his own fears. Hands folded, he reports to Ram that a recognised thief will try to kill, and having said so he is at rest.
core_teaching: Striving can paradoxically increase the distance; what holds is not the striving but the unchanging nature of the Lord and the fact of belonging to him.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Reads: the more I want to come near, the farther I go; you are the same in all four ages and I have remained yours though full of sin; the vile age tricked me and turned gold to base metal.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Explains that every effort to come close becomes an obstacle through maya's contact; notes the eternal tie of Brahman and jiva; says he was a part of pure being-consciousness-bliss reduced by the senses to something worth two cowries.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: the more I wish to draw closer to you, the farther away I get; you are steadfast in essence through all four ages, and I'm yours though filled with faults.

practical_reading: For people who try hard at spiritual or personal growth and feel worse: effort that becomes anxious can push us away; rest in belonging rather than performance.
misreadings: Not an argument that effort is pointless; it is about the paradox of anxious striving.
Grace does not erase responsibility (our misuse note).
cautions: 'Turned gold into base metal, king into beggar' may resonate painfully with someone who lost status or wealth.
speaks_to: trying harder and feeling further away
spiritual dryness
feeling full of faults yet wanting to belong

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 267, stanza 1 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 267, Haritoshini 267, Thakur 267.
translation_note: Accurate. 'प्रभु की सौं करि निबर्‍यो हौं' - Poddar reads it as 'I have sworn by the Lord'; our 'I swear by the Lord, I have lain down here' is fine.
context: Tulsi stages a sit-in (dharna) at Ram's door: he has vowed not to get up his whole life until Ram says 'you are mine'. Yama's messengers pushed him till they tired and couldn't move him; he endured the womb's agony in birth after birth and came out of hell in defiance. Like a child who has dug in for a toy, he will take what he wants, because Ram is kind; he asks Ram to say it quickly, since he is melting with embarrassment, and if Ram is ashamed to say it publicly because of Tulsi's faults, he could say it quietly.

key_terms.sense: lying at Ram's door (a sit-in, dharna)

core_teaching: Devotion can be stubborn: the devotee refuses to leave until he is acknowledged, trusting the Lord's kindness to give in.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I have vowed to lie at your door and won't rise my whole life until you say 'you are mine', sworn by you; Yama's messengers tired of pushing me.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Calls it Tulsi's satyagraha: he sits in dharna at Ram's door until told 'you are mine', even if life passes.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: having vowed from today to lie at Rama's door, I shall not rise while I live until he tells me 'You are mine'; death's messengers are weary of pushing me away.

practical_reading: Legitimises persistence in prayer and in seeking acknowledgment: it's all right to keep asking, even stubbornly.
misreadings: Not a model for refusing to leave a person's door who has said no; it is addressed to God.
Surrender follows effort and reflection, not instead of it (our misuse note).
cautions: References to hell and the agony of the womb in stanza 2.
Could be misapplied to human relationships where persistence becomes harassment.
speaks_to: needing to be acknowledged
persistence in prayer
feeling ignored but unwilling to give up
not_for: someone fixated on a person who has rejected them

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 268, stanzas 1 and 4 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 268, Haritoshini 268, Thakur 268.
translation_note: Accurate.
context: Tulsi sets his own test for being accepted: when the mind turns around and loves the Lord without guile with the same natural ease it now clings to pleasures. Stanza 2: when it loves Ram as one loves a son, trusts him as a friend, fears him as a king, and holds to him alone like the chataka bird to rain-cloud. Stanza 3: when honour does not elate it nor insult burn it, and it is even in loss and gain, joy and sorrow. Stanza 4: when hearing Ram's qualities brings joy and tears, Tulsi will trust he has become Ram's, and joy will fill his heart.

key_terms.sense: with the same natural ease (with which it clung to pleasures)
tears will flow from the eyes

core_teaching: The sign of being accepted by God is inner: the heart's natural pull redirected toward the divine, shown in steadiness and spontaneous joy and tears at hearing of him.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I'll know you have made me yours when my mind turns to you; when it loves you without guile as naturally as it now clings to sense objects.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same bhavartha, adding that while one is a slave of desire one cannot be Ram's servant. Its note on the preceding pada describes the devotee's child-like insistence and urgency to reach the Lord before death.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: then shall I know for sure you've made me yours, when my mind turns towards you with the natural ease it takes to sense objects, loving you spontaneously and abandoning all deceit.

practical_reading: A gentle self-check: notice where your attention naturally goes, and ask for that same ease to turn toward what you love most.
misreadings: Not a requirement to feel tears or ecstasy as proof of faith.
Not a reason to doubt acceptance when feelings are dry; it is Tulsi's longing, not a test for others.
cautions: Could make someone who feels nothing in prayer worry they are rejected; frame as hope, not criterion.
speaks_to: wanting your heart to change, not just your behaviour
noticing where your mind naturally goes
longing for real feeling in faith
not_for: someone anxious about whether God accepts them (it sets conditions)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 270, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 270, Thakur 270. (Haritoshini's 270 could not be cleanly isolated in the OCR text.)
translation_note: Accurate. 'अवगुन अमित बितैहो' - Poddar reads it as 'will you end/destroy my countless faults'; Thakur 'bring my faults to an end'. Our 'let my faults go' is a fair paraphrase.
context: Tulsi asks whether Ram will ever look his way, knowing that good or bad he is Ram's own, and put an end to his countless faults. In birth after birth the mind has defeated him; will Ram now let him win? Then Tulsi would have a master, and Ram would earn his name 'lord of the masterless', if he isn't put off by Tulsi's smallness. He asks out of his own fear: Ram is his master, guru, mother, father - everything - so whom else can he tell?

key_terms.sense: will you look at me too
good or bad, your own servant

core_teaching: Belonging comes before goodness: one is Ram's own, good or bad, and that relationship is the basis for asking that faults be removed.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: will you, merciful one, look at me, knowing that whatever I am I am your servant, and end my endless faults; in every birth the mind has beaten me, now let me win.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: will you look towards me in compassion and, knowing that good or ill I'm your own servant, bring my unnumbered faults to an end.

practical_reading: For someone ashamed of repeated failures: start from 'I still belong', then ask for help to win against the habits that keep winning.
misreadings: Not a dismissal of responsibility for faults; the plea is to have them ended, not ignored.
speaks_to: shame about repeated failures
feeling unseen
losing the same inner battle again and again
research_note: Haritoshini extract for 270 was mixed with neighbouring padas in the OCR; not used.

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 271, stanzas 1 and 4 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 271, Thakur 271. (Haritoshini's 271 could not be cleanly isolated in the OCR text.)
translation_note: Accurate. 'ढरनि आपनी ढरिये' = follow your own natural way of melting/showing mercy; 'keep to your own nature' is good. The last image: a broken arm is still bound up at the neck (in a sling), and an injured eye, when it aches, is still treated (Poddar).
context: Tulsi asks Ram, ocean of mercy and protector of refugees, not to cast him off: whatever he is, he is Ram's servant. Others (his vices) have already ruined him, so do not ruin him further; Ram has always mended everyone's affairs, so mend his too. Why fear the world's laughter at taking him in? Treat him with the same nature that made friends of monkeys and a boatman. Guilty as he is, he is Ram's own: a broken arm is still slung from the neck, and a damaged eye is still cared for when it hurts.

key_terms.sense: act according to your own merciful nature
even a broken arm is hung from the neck (in a sling)

key_terms.term: फूटेहु बिलोचन पीर होत हित करिये
key_terms.sense: even a damaged eye, when it aches, is cared for

core_teaching: One does not discard a part of oneself because it is broken; in the same way the Lord does not discard a faulty devotee who is still his own.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: whatever I am I'm yours, don't forsake me; I am already spoiled by lust and anger, don't spoil me more; you have always mended everyone; don't fear the world's mockery; though guilty I am yours.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: however I may be I'm your servant, do not forsake me; already ruined by others, be not angry with one lost; though I have done wrong I am still yours; even a broken arm is cared for.

practical_reading: A powerful image for anyone who feels broken or useless: what is damaged is held closer, not thrown away. Also a model for how families and communities treat their struggling members.
misreadings: Not saying the person is useless; the image is about being kept and tended because one belongs.
cautions: Injury imagery (broken arm, damaged eye) may be literal for someone recently injured or disabled; it can comfort but should be handled carefully.
speaks_to: feeling broken or like a burden
after a failure that made you feel discarded
family members who feel like the 'problem'
illness or injury
research_note: Haritoshini extract for 271 was mixed with neighbouring padas in the OCR; not used.

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 273, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 273, Haritoshini 273, Thakur 273.
translation_note: Accurate. 'सहज छोह' = natural, unprompted tenderness (Viyogi Hari: causeless, desireless affection).
context: Tulsi asks whom else he could tell, who else wishes him well, who else has natural tenderness for servant, friend, sufferer and orphan. Many fallen people crossed the ocean of the world without boat or raft simply because Ram glanced at them - in grace or anger, in sincerity, by accident or sideways. Whichever glance Ram likes, let him cast it quickly on Tulsi and make him his own without delay, for the end of life is very near.

key_terms.sense: the suffering, the one with no protector

core_teaching: Divine tenderness is natural, not earned; a single glance of any kind from Ram is enough to carry someone across.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: leaving you, whom do I tell, who is my friend; who else has natural kindness for servant, friend, sufferer and orphan; many sinners crossed without boat because you looked at them in grace, anger, sincerity, by mistake or askance.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Says elsewhere one finds only the self-interested; maps the glances to stories: grace to Ahalya and Jatayu, anger to Ravana and Kansa, sincerity to Guha, Sugriva and Vibhishana, accident to the Yavana.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: leaving you whom shall I tell; who else is a friend to his servant, whose grace falls naturally on the afflicted and orphaned; delay not, for life's end is very near.

practical_reading: Encourages someone who feels uncared for to bring their need directly, trusting a tenderness that does not depend on merit.
misreadings: Not saying human friends are worthless.
cautions: The full pada ends with 'life's end is near'; avoid for readers who are seriously ill or elderly and anxious about death, unless chosen deliberately.
speaks_to: feeling that no one wishes you well
loneliness
needing tenderness
not_for: someone frightened about approaching death (stanza 3)

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 274, stanza 1 (of 3) - Gita Press/Poddar 274, Haritoshini 274, Thakur 274.
translation_note: Accurate in sense. 'सब अँग बल-बिहीन' Poddar and Viyogi Hari read as without strength in any of the means (sadhanas), i.e. utterly without resources; Thakur reads it more literally ('devoid of all strength and all limbs'). Our 'every limb has lost its strength' is literal and fine; note the commentators' figurative sense. Our line ('there is still a place where you are kept') is a gentle paraphrase.
context: Tulsi asks where a sorrowful, poor person can go: who is a master as kind as Ram, who keeps a refugee with no strength left in any part? Other masters take in servants who are rich, talented and serve well; caring for the poor, the talentless and the lazy suits only Ram. Ram knows his heart already; for one as foul-minded as Tulsi, Ram is the only support in three worlds and three times.

key_terms.sense: one who has come for refuge
without strength in any limb / any means

core_teaching: Worldly masters accept the capable; Ram accepts those who have nothing left to offer.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: where shall I go, who is so kind as to shelter a refugee with no strength in any spiritual means; other masters take the rich, virtuous and good servants.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; quotes Vyasa's lament 'at whose door shall I go'; argues 'navin' is an epithet of Ram (ever-young), against commentators who read 'who new would care for the poor'.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: whither shall I go, where is place for a wretched and sorrowful one; who is compassionate like you, who could accept this refuge-seeker devoid of all strength and limbs.

practical_reading: For people exhausted by illness, grief or burnout: when you have nothing to give, you can still be kept.
misreadings: Not an endorsement of laziness; it describes being accepted without merit.
cautions: Literal reading ('every limb has lost its strength') may touch readers with disability or chronic illness; it can comfort, but avoid implying illness is a moral state.

illness or weakness
feeling you have nothing to offer
burnout

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 275, stanzas 1, 3 and 4 (of 4) - Gita Press/Poddar 275, Haritoshini 275, Thakur 275.
translation_note: Accurate. 'काढ़ि रद' = baring the teeth, i.e. begging abjectly. 'रघुबर ओर बिनाहूँ' Poddar reads as Ram not abandoning even those with no other side/support; fine. Note the omitted stanza 2 says his parents abandoned him at birth like a snake its young.
context: Tulsi recalls begging from door to door, grinning and falling at feet; the world has kind people able to end sorrow, yet none even spoke to him. His parents left him as a snake leaves its newborn; he blames no one but his own luck, and people shrank from touching his shadow. Seeing his misery, saints told him not to worry: Ram has never cast off even beasts, low ones and sinners who came for shelter. From then on Tulsi became Ram's and was happy, even without much love or faith; seeing what the name's glory and the Lord's gentleness have done for him, he is shy and amazed.

key_terms.sense: told my need at door after door
conversation; no one even spoke to him
I feel shy, and I marvel

core_teaching: After universal rejection, a word from good people pointed Tulsi to a refuge that does not reject; he became happy there even before his love and faith were mature.

commentaries.who: Hanuman Prasad Poddar, Gita Press bhavartha (Vinay Patrika, 2001 ed.)
commentaries.gist: Explains: I begged at every door, but no one spoke; my parents abandoned me like a snake its young; I blame my fate; people shrank from my shadow.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Same reading; discusses the text variant ('tanu-janyo' vs 'tvacha'): Baijnath and Bhatt read it as a snake shedding its skin, but he prefers the Nagari Pracharini reading of a snake abandoning its newborn.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: door to door I told of my wretchedness, baring my teeth and prostrating, yet no one spoke to me; my parents cast me away; a holy man said 'grieve not'.

practical_reading: For someone who has been turned away repeatedly: one kind voice can point to a place of acceptance; you need not wait until your faith feels strong to be held.
misreadings: Not saying the rejection was deserved; Tulsi blames 'luck', not character.
Grace does not erase responsibility (our misuse note).
cautions: Explicit parental abandonment and social untouchability ('shrank from my shadow') in stanza 2; potentially raw for adoptees or people who faced caste or family rejection.
speaks_to: repeated rejection
feeling unworthy of help
being pointed to help by a kind person
gratitude and wonder at unexpected grace
not_for: someone currently homeless or begging who needs practical help, if used in place of it

verified_ref: Vinaya Patrika pada 191, doha 8 (of 9) - Haritoshini 191 (OCR '१६१'), Thakur 191; Gita Press 2001 prints pada 191 with the same opening ('एक सनेही साँचिलो केवल कोसलपालु') but its commentary on this couplet was not legible in the OCR.
translation_note: Accurate. 'गाँठी बाँध्यो दाम' = tied money in the knot of one's cloth (the way coins were carried); 'परख्यो न फेरि खर-खोट' = never assayed again whether genuine or counterfeit (Viyogi Hari: as one ties money without testing it, whether good or bad). Thakur: put in the purse and not taken out to examine.
context: Pada 191 is a sequence of dohas on Ram as the one true lover: body-companions are self-interested, gods are business-like, and the classic objects of love in poetry fail their lovers (sound kills the deer, fire burns the moth, water does not die for the fish, the moon ignores the chakor, the cloud pelts the chataka with hail). Ram alone honours love, embraced the boatman like his brother Bharata, and makes the unlucky lucky. Doha 8 (our lines): whoever took refuge in his name, however low, he kept like money tied in his cloth, never checked again. Doha 9: he took in even Tulsi, whose deeds make other sinners.

key_terms.sense: tied the coin into the knot of his cloth: kept it as his own

core_teaching: Once someone takes shelter in the name, Ram keeps them without re-examining their worth: acceptance is not a probation.

commentaries.who: Viyogi Hari, Haritoshini tika (bhavartha and tippani), Sahitya Seva Sadan, Kashi
commentaries.gist: Reads the doha: whoever took shelter in his name, however low and sinful, he accepted as one ties money in a knot without testing it, genuine or false.

commentaries.who: M. M. Thakur, The Vinaya Patrika: An English Rendering (reading of the line, not a commentary)
commentaries.gist: Renders: however great a sinner, whoever took the Name's refuge was accepted by him, just as a coin is put in the purse and not taken out again to examine it.

practical_reading: Speaks to people who feel they are always being tested and found wanting: in this love, one is not re-weighed every day.
misreadings: Grace does not erase responsibility or consequences (our misuse note).
Not a claim that the person is 'counterfeit'; the image is about not testing.
cautions: Calling someone 'low' or 'sinful' may sting; lead with the coin image.
speaks_to: feeling constantly judged or on probation
imposter syndrome
fear of being found out
